AuDiR: Diagnosing Audio Reasoning
with Rule and Percept Interventions

Chengwei Wei    Yi Ma    and Nancy F. Chen ††thanks: C. Wei and N. F. Chen are with the Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing (IAIC) and the Centre for Frontier AI Research (CFAR), Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), Singapore.††thanks: Y. Ma is with the Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing (IAIC), Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), Singapore.††thanks: Corresponding author: Chengwei Wei (e-mail: chengwei7272@gmail.com).
Abstract

Answer accuracy alone does not distinguish failures in acoustic perception, rule knowledge, and rule application. AuDiR (Audio Diagnostic Reasoning) examines these distinctions through controlled input interventions. Each item contains an audio clip, a multiple-choice question, a task-general rule, and a textual description of the acoustic observations needed to answer. Three conditions progressively supply the rule and observations; a fourth removes the audio while retaining the question and rule. The first correct diagnostic condition assigns an operational response label, without identifying a unique internal cause. The current benchmark contains 201 items in 18 families drawn from 9 sources, with answer references documented separately from percept extraction. In a preliminary evaluation of Gemini-3.8-flash, accuracy is 29.3% without supplied information, 31.3% with the rule, and 98.5% with the observations also supplied. No-audio accuracy is 23.9%, with a confidence interval containing the 25.0% chance rate. A family-level knowledge probe associates incomplete rule recall with larger gains from rule provision. These results show the benefit of supplying acoustic observations as text, while incomplete validation, possible recognition shortcuts, and non-monotonic responses limit stronger failure-attribution claims.

Index Terms: 
Audio reasoning, diagnostic evaluation, benchmark construction, dataset, large audio language models.

I Introduction

Audio reasoning benchmarks such as MMAR [1], MMAU [2] and STAR-Bench [3] measure whether a model answers correctly. Accuracy alone does not distinguish among three possible sources of error:

  • •

    Missing knowledge. The model did not know the rule the task needs: that a passing car’s tone shift gives its speed, or that a shaft tone at ff Hz means 60​f60f RPM.

  • •

    Failed perception. The model knew the rule but did not recover the quantity the rule consumes from the audio.

  • •

    Failed application. The model had the rule and the quantity and still reached the wrong answer.

Answer scores alone cannot separate these cases. Post-hoc analysis can provide additional information: MMAR manually categorizes a sample of failed predictions as perceptual, knowledge, reasoning, or other errors. Such analysis requires annotation and relies on the model’s written explanation, which need not reflect the computation that produced its answer.

AuDiR (Audio Diagnostic Reasoning) makes the attribution part of the item instead. We write each item as three separable parts: a rule that can be stated in language, an acoustic observation to be recovered from the clip, and a question that needs the rule applied to the percept. We then run the item under three diagnostic conditions: audio and question alone, then with the rule, then with the percept text as well. The first correct condition assigns a response-pattern label associated with capability, knowledge or perception; failure under all three is assigned to application. The interpretation depends on the supplied information being sufficient and correct, and does not assume that responses improve monotonically. A fourth, separate condition removes the audio to probe answerability from the question and rule alone.

The protocol records responses to four controlled inputs for every item. This reduces the need for post-hoc annotation of model explanations, although constructing and validating the items still requires human work.

We contribute:

  • •

    An item design and operational diagnostic protocol: rule, percept, and question as separate fields, evaluated under three diagnostic conditions and one control (Section III).

  • •

    A construction procedure that separates percept extraction from answer references and documents rejected candidate pairings (Section IV-C).

  • •

    A benchmark build with explicit provenance and contamination flags, and no-audio responses reported in aggregate (Sections IV-B and V-D).

  • •

    A preliminary evaluation of Gemini-3.8-flash over all 201 items, including intervention response profiles and a family-level knowledge-recall probe (Sections V and VI).

II Related Work

II-A Audio reasoning benchmarks

Benchmarks for large audio language models have grown quickly in size and in the range of skills they cover. AIR-Bench [4] pairs roughly 19k single-choice questions over nineteen foundation tasks with 2k open-ended items. MMAU [2] assembles 10k clips over speech, environmental sound and music, annotated for 27 skills. MMAR [1] takes the opposite trade and curates 1,000 audio–question–answer triplets from real videos, filtered through repeated correction passes, with a deliberate tail of items needing graduate-level domain knowledge. STAR-Bench [3] narrows the target to spatio-temporal and physical reasoning and, like us, uses synthesized and physics-simulated audio so that the governing quantity is known exactly.

These benchmarks differ in scope, but their answer scores do not directly separate the three failure modes considered here.

Audio necessity is better served than failure attribution, though only in aggregate. MMAU replaces the audio with Gaussian noise and reports that some models are barely affected. MMAR runs the same substitution and finds that every model degrades, while noting that one still scores above chance on noise alone, which it attributes to a residual language prior that survived a three-stage review. STAR-Bench substitutes machine-generated captions for the audio and reports that caption-only answering costs MMAU only 5.9% and MMAR 9.0%, against 31.5% and 35.2% on its own items, and uses the contrast to argue that earlier benchmarks test what text can already carry. All three are model-level diagnostics run on a finished benchmark. None is an admission test: an item that survives the substitution is reported, not removed. AuDiR includes an explicit no-audio condition in its construction framework. The current evaluation reports this control in aggregate; implementing a validated per-item admission test remains further work.

II-B Stage-level failure attribution

Three routes to a stage-level diagnosis exist, and all three are applied after the benchmark is built.

The first reads the model’s output. MMAR [1] has annotators read 100 failed predictions from one model and label each as a perceptual, knowledge, reasoning or other error. This provides useful error categories, but requires manual annotation and interprets written explanations rather than observing internal computation.

The second reads aggregate score patterns. STAR-Bench [3] evaluates nineteen models and concludes that proprietary systems are bottlenecked by fine-grained perception while open models lag across perception, knowledge and reasoning together. The vocabulary is close to ours and the evidence is not per item: the conclusion is inferred from how model averages move across task families, so it describes a model on a benchmark rather than a model on an item, and it cannot say which items would be fixed by which intervention.

The third opens the model. SonicBench [5], concurrent with this work, isolates twelve low-level physical attributes such as pitch, loudness and spatial location, synthesizes stimuli in which each is controlled, and asks binary questions about it. Most audio language models sit near the 0.50 chance rate where human listeners reach 0.91, and explicit reasoning adds little. SonicBench then localizes the loss by probing: a two-layer probe on the frozen final encoder output, trained per attribute, reaches 60% or better even where the end-to-end model answers at chance, so the cue is present in the representation and the loss occurs after the encoder.

Representation probing and input interventions provide different evidence. Probing tests whether an acoustic attribute can be decoded from model representations and requires access to those representations. AuDiR instead tests whether supplying a rule or observation changes the answer, so it can also be applied to API-only models. A correct answer after supplying percept text does not identify where information was lost within the model.

Caption substitution and AuDiR’s percept condition also differ. A caption summarizes a clip; our percept text states the observations selected for a particular question. The separate no-audio condition retains neither the clip nor these observations. It probes text-only answerability in aggregate, without certifying individual items as shortcut-free. The protocol is limited to tasks whose required observations can be expressed in text.

II-C Diagnostic datasets and input ablation

Building a dataset so that its errors are interpretable has a long precedent outside audio. CLEVR [6] generates scenes and questions from a known grammar, so a failure can be traced to a specific reasoning operation. HANS [7] constructs inference cases in which a named heuristic gives the wrong answer, making reliance on it visible in the score. CheckList [8] tests capabilities separately instead of reporting one aggregate. AuDiR follows this line with a different controlled variable: not the structure of the input, but how much of the solution is handed over.

Our fourth condition belongs to a second established family. Hypothesis-only baselines showed that a large share of natural language inference items could be classified without reading the premise [9, 10], and the same logic motivated rebalancing visual question answering so that answers could not be recovered from the question’s language prior alone [11, 12]. Removing the input the task is nominally about, and observing that performance survives, is what exposed the shortcut. AuDiR combines this control with explicit rule and percept interventions. The control probes text-only answerability, while the diagnostic conditions describe how responses change when information is supplied.

Table I places AuDiR against the audio benchmarks above on the two axes that matter here. The systems all of this targets are audio-conditioned language models [13, 14, 15, 16, 17]; Section VI reports the preliminary evaluation of one model.

III The AuDiR Benchmark

III-A Overview

AuDiR evaluates audio reasoning through controlled changes to the information supplied to a model. Each multiple-choice item combines an audio clip and a question with a task-general rule and a textual representation of the relevant acoustic observations. Three diagnostic conditions progressively supply the rule and the observations; a fourth condition removes the audio to probe text-only answerability. The first successful diagnostic condition defines an operational diagnosis: a label for the observed response pattern, whose interpretation depends on the quality of the supplied information.

The current build contains 201 items in 18 families drawn from 9 sources. This section defines the item components, the input conditions, the assignment rule and the record format of an item. Section IV describes the sources, the composition they yield and the construction procedure; Section V reports the baseline evaluation.

III-B Knowledge, percept, and question

The item design separates the observation to be recovered from the rule that consumes it. Let AA denote the audio and QQ the question, its answer choices and any stated constants. The three components have distinct roles:

  • •

    Knowledge (KK) states a rule shared across a task family. It may include general constants, but not the item’s acoustic observations or target answer.

  • •

    Percept (PP) states the item-specific observations that a listener would need to recover from AA, such as two frequencies or an onset and an offset. This text is withheld in the base condition.

  • •

    Question (QQ) asks for a conclusion obtained by applying KK to those observations. Item-specific non-acoustic givens are included here and kept fixed across conditions.

Example (vehicle speed). The audio is a car passing a roadside microphone at constant speed. The percept is the pair of engine-tone frequencies heard while the car approaches and recedes. The question is “how fast was the car moving?” The knowledge is the Doppler relation, fa=f0​c/(c−v)f_{a}=f_{0}c/(c-v) while approaching and fr=f0​c/(c+v)f_{r}=f_{0}c/(c+v) while receding, with c≈343c\approx 343 m/s. Applying this relation to the two frequencies gives a speed estimate, which is mapped to an answer bin. The gold bin is determined separately from the speed the driver held on cruise control during that pass, which VS13 records alongside the audio, rather than from an audio-based speed estimate. Fig. 1 illustrates the audio-based prediction path and the independent measurement path used to obtain the gold answer.

Three requirements govern the intended decomposition. First, KK must be task-general and free of item-specific observations and answers. Second, PP, together with the givens in QQ, must supply all observations needed to apply KK. Third, PP must preserve the claimed application step: it should state observations rather than the target answer. These are requirements to audit, not guarantees provided by the field names. In particular, an event-rate percept must include duration as well as count, and a category question must not receive its answer directly in the percept field (Section III-D).

Ground-truth provenance is a separate requirement. The gold answer should come from an independent measurement or a quantity fixed by construction, rather than from the same audio estimator used to write PP. An externally supplied annotation is not by itself proof of this independence; its derivation must also be documented (Section IV-C).

III-C The four conditions

Table II specifies the complete inputs. Each condition is a separate inference run, with the same question, choices and scoring rule. Conditions ①–③ add information cumulatively; condition ④ is a separate control, not a further step in that sequence. In the vehicle example, ② adds the Doppler rule, ③ also states the two frequencies, and ④ retains the question and rule but supplies neither audio nor percept text.

Condition ④ probes whether the question and rule support answering without audio. Its direct audio ablation is relative to ②; comparing ③ with ④ changes both audio and percept text. A single correct no-audio answer may be a guess and does not establish leakage. We therefore report aggregate control accuracy against the chance rate implied by the choices. The present results do not certify individual items as free of text-only shortcuts (Section V-D).

III-D Operational diagnostic assignment

Let zjz_{j} indicate whether the response under diagnostic condition jj is correct. We assign each model–item pair to the first successful condition in the order ①, ②, ③. The correctness patterns (z1,z2,z3)(z_{1},z_{2},z_{3}) define four disjoint groups:

  • •

    1∗∗1**: capable, correct without supplied information;

  • •

    01∗01*: missing knowledge, first correct with the rule supplied;

  • •

    001001: failed perception, first correct with observations also supplied;

  • •

    000000: failed application, incorrect under all three conditions.

Here ∗* denotes either outcome. Fig. 2(b) visualizes this assignment. The labels summarize responses to interventions; they do not establish a unique internal cause or identify a particular model component. In particular, an item answered correctly under ① remains in the capable group even if a later condition is incorrect. Non-monotonic responses must therefore be examined alongside the four group sizes.

The intended interpretation requires a correct, usable rule and sufficient, accurate percept text. Supplying a rule may also change prompting or attention, and a correct multiple-choice answer need not reflect a successful reasoning chain. Likewise, an incomplete PP can leave perception necessary under ③, whereas a PP that states the answer can bypass application. Earlier builds contained event-rate percepts without duration and category percepts that named the answer. These examples motivate checking the sufficiency of PP and whether it preserves an application step. The current results should be read with the validation coverage reported in Section IV-C4.

III-E Item schema

Each item is stored as a record carrying its identifier and family; the source, license, and a contamination flag; the question, choices, and gold answer; the knowledge string; and percept_name and percept_text, the latter being the sentence inserted at condition ③. The four materialized prompts are stored alongside, so a third party can reproduce the exact input the model saw without rerunning the pipeline. The local build associates one audio clip with each item.

The proposed release separates item records and analysis code from source audio. Audio packaging will follow the terms of each source, including for transformed recordings. Where redistribution is not permitted, the intended package provides source identifiers, time spans and transformation instructions for local reconstruction. Source-specific permissions and the final licences for release materials remain to be confirmed; this manuscript does not constitute a released dataset.

III-F Contamination

Items carry contamination-risk flags. Newly synthesized audio reduces the risk of exposure to the exact clip, but does not eliminate shortcuts in question templates or answer choices. Research corpora without published question–answer pairs are marked as lower risk; this is a provenance-based flag, not a measured guarantee.

The current build retains one MMAR well-depth item whose question, answer and explanation are public. It is included in the reported totals and marked as high risk. We retain it as a case study, not as a validated positive control. A single item cannot establish the power of the no-audio condition to detect contamination. That requires a separate contamination set and comparisons with unflagged items.

IV Data and construction

This section describes where AuDiR’s audio and its answers come from. One requirement governs the whole procedure: an item’s answer must be checkable against a measurement that the audio did not produce. That requirement, rather than audio quality or item count, is what limits the size of the benchmark, and it holds per target quantity rather than per corpus, so the same recordings are admitted for some questions and rejected for others. We report the sources in the current build, the composition they yield, the construction procedure that turns an admitted pairing into items, the pairings that procedure rejected, and the families being recorded to replace them.

IV-A Sources in use

Table III lists the 9 sources behind the current build. They fall into four kinds according to where the answer comes from: an instrument recorded beside the microphone, a physical measurement of the object, an annotation produced outside any acoustic estimator, or a quantity set by the experimenter before the audio existed. What follows states, for each source, what the recordings are, how its answer reference was obtained, and what we did and did not build from it. None of these corpora was assembled for reasoning evaluation; each is admitted for the specific quantities whose provenance survives inspection.

VS13 [18] records single vehicles driving past a camera and microphone at the roadside, thirteen passenger cars chosen to differ in manufacturer, year, engine and transmission, over four hundred passes between 30 and 105 km/h. The speed of each pass is the speed the driver held on the car’s cruise control, which the corpus reports is stable for at least three seconds either side of the pass-by; it is logged per file, together with the instant the car leaves the camera frame, which approximates the closest point of approach. That speed is set before the recording and is not derived from the sound, which is what admits the source, but it is the vehicle’s own reading of itself rather than a roadside measurement, and a speedometer is permitted to read high. We build the two Doppler families from it and use no other quantity.

Sound of Water [19] records water being poured into fifty-one vessels, each measured with a ruler: top and bottom internal diameter, net internal height, and for some the wall thickness. Each of its recordings names the vessel it used and carries flags for a constant pour and a clean recording, both of which we require. The geometry is the answer reference for both families we build, container height and the taller/fuller comparison, and it is a measurement of the object rather than of the sound. The corpus ships no pitch annotation, so the percept is measured by us and checked against the geometry rather than the other way round. Two thirds of the vessels are visibly tapered, which is why volume is computed as a truncated cone and why the comparison family states the radius in the question.

GuitarSet [20] records solo and accompaniment guitar takes with a hexaphonic pickup, one channel per string, alongside the ordinary mixed recording. The note, chord, beat and key annotations are derived from the per-string channels, so they do not come from the signal a model is given. We build three families on the mixed recording: the interval between two notes, the quality of a four-note chord, and the major key of a passage. The same recordings also supply the unmodified notes that the detuning family transforms.

AudioTime [21] is constructed audio in which the onset and offset of every sound event are fixed when the clip is assembled rather than annotated afterwards, which makes the event timestamps exact by construction. We use the event counts and clip durations for the two event-rate families. We do not use the timestamps themselves as an answer, because a question about when something happened is answered by reading the timestamp rather than by applying a rule.

MAFAULDA [22] records a rotating machine under induced fault conditions with a tachometer channel recorded simultaneously with the microphones. The tachometer is a sensor independent of the microphone, which makes the rotation rate the strongest ground truth in the build. We use it for absolute rotation speed and the speed ratio between two machines. We do not build the fault-diagnosis question the corpus was made for: the bearing fault frequencies sit within a fraction of a hertz of the shaft harmonics at these speeds, which fails C5.

Hillenbrand vowels [23] records isolated American English vowels read by men, women, boys and girls at 16 kHz, with formant tracks supplied every 10 ms. The vowel label is what the speaker was asked to produce, not what an analyzer decided afterwards, so it is independent of any acoustic measurement. We build vowel identity from the first two formants and a formant chart stated per speaker group.

CirCor DigiScope [24] records heart sounds from nearly a thousand paediatric patients at up to four auscultation sites, with each recording segmented by clinicians into the first heart sound, systole, the second heart sound and diastole. The segmentation is expert annotation rather than an algorithm’s output. We build heart rate from the instants of the heart sounds, which requires the rule that a beat produces two sounds and that the rate follows the gap between successive first sounds, not between successive sounds.

Controlled transformation of a real recording supplies the families whose target quantity does not exist in any corpus we could find. A recorded engine is flown past a virtual microphone at a chosen speed and distance; a recorded guitar note is detuned by a chosen number of cents against an unmodified copy of itself; a recorded pour or pass-by is band-limited to a chosen sampling rate and converted back up. The transformation parameter is exact because it was fixed before the audio was rendered, and the sound remains a real engine, guitar or pour rather than a synthesized tone. 48 of 201 items are built this way. The limitation is stated in Section VII: a rule that the renderer applied is a rule the item cannot test for truth, only for application.

MMAR [1] contributes one item, retained deliberately. Its question, answer and chain of thought are public, so it is flagged as contaminated, counted in every total, and read as a case study rather than as a positive control on the leak test.

Licences differ, and one source does not permit redistribution of audio, so the release is partly by fetch script rather than a single archive.

IV-B Families and perceptual axes

Table IV lists the 18 families these sources yield, including the flagged contamination case of Section III-F. Together they hold 23 minutes of audio (mean 6.8 s, median 3.5 s, range 0.1–48 s). All 201 items have four choices, giving a uniform-guessing accuracy of 25.0%. The question forms comprise 95 absolute estimates, 60 classifications and 46 comparisons or ratios. Counts and durations refer to the current item set.

A family is an item template: one source, one percept, one rule. A perceptual axis groups the observations to be recovered, such as a pitch pattern, an event time or a decay tail. An axis can group multiple families, providing a way to organize response profiles by perceptual demand. In the current build, most axes occur in only one source, so axis effects cannot generally be separated from source effects. Table V reports this organization, not evidence of cross-source generalization.

IV-C Construction pipeline

Fig. 2 summarizes admission and the subsequent diagnostic assignment. The pipeline has seven stages. Its binding constraint is not audio quality or item count but ground-truth provenance, and most candidate work is eliminated at stage two. One property guides construction: the percept text and gold answer should follow separate derivation paths. What can be heard determines condition ③’s text; an independent reference determines the answer. This avoids treating agreement with an audio estimator as independent correctness. The provenance of shipped annotations requires further documentation to establish this separation for every current family.

IV-C1 Candidate sourcing as percept–target pairing

We select candidate percept–target pairs from available recordings. A candidate is one (percept, target quantity) pairing: something a human can hear, and something reachable from it by a stated rule. One recording source can yield several pairings, and they are admitted or rejected independently. Sound of Water, for instance, supports container height but not fill rate, and Table III and Table VI list the same corpus on both sides.

IV-C2 Admission test

Candidate pairings are screened against the following design criteria:

  • C1

    Percept present. the cue the rule consumes is actually audible to a human, at the recording’s bandwidth and noise floor.

  • C2

    Audio-necessary. the answer cannot be reached from the question text, the file name, or dataset priors.

  • C3

    Real reasoning step. the rule must be applied. A pairing where the percept is the answer tests recognition, not reasoning.

  • C4

    Independent ground truth. the answer is checked against a measurement that does not derive from the signal being analyzed.

  • C5

    Measurable. the percept can be recovered from the audio reliably enough that a correct chain reaches the correct answer.

C4 is the criterion that rejects most candidates, and it deserves emphasis because it is easy to violate accidentally. A ground truth estimated from the same signal the model is asked to analyze is circular: the item then certifies only that our estimator and the model agree, and a model that hears perfectly but disagrees with our estimator is scored wrong. An item can satisfy the other design criteria while still relying on an inaccurate reference. Reference provenance therefore needs a separate check.

Table VI records rejected candidate pairings and the criteria they failed.

IV-C3 Percept extraction and ground-truth binding

For an admitted pairing we extract the percept value from the audio and bind the answer to the independent ground truth. These are two separate operations on two separate sources. The percept is what a careful listener could obtain, and it is used only to write condition ③’s text. The answer comes from the instrument, annotation, or construction listed in Table IV. The ground truths in AuDiR are of four kinds. An instrument independent of the microphone (a tachometer channel recorded beside it), a physical measurement of the object (container geometry by ruler), a shipped annotation produced outside our pipeline (event timestamps, note transcription), and control, where the quantity is set before the audio exists, either by the experimenter during recording (a driver holding cruise control at a stated speed) or by rendering (a pass-by synthesized at a chosen speed and distance). A control is only as good as the setting is faithful: a cruise-control speed is the vehicle’s own reading of itself, and a speedometer is permitted to read high. Being external to our pipeline does not establish that an annotation is independent of the analyzed signal; that provenance must be audited. The retained MMAR case has only a dataset-provided answer documented here and should not be read as an instrument-validated item.

IV-C4 Percept extraction and verification

The percept sentence is produced by a measurement routine written for the family, not by a person listening and describing. Pitches and pitch shifts come from a fundamental-frequency tracker run over the clip and read at the instants the rule needs. Event counts and instants come from an onset detector, bounded by the source’s own timestamps where it ships them. Levels come from short-time energy in decibels relative to full scale. Bandwidth comes from the highest frequency carrying appreciable energy in the long-term spectrum. Formants come from linear prediction. The routine writes one sentence per item from a fixed template, so the wording varies only where the numbers do.

Errors in percept text can affect the interpretation of condition ③. We use three checks: applying the stated rule to the percept, re-measuring the audio using another method, and comparison with a standard tool where available. The stored check records cover 189 of 201 current items; the 12 heart-rate items have no records in these three checks.

Rule application agrees with gold on 129 items and disagrees on 0, with 60 marked not applicable. Re-measurement agrees on 79, disagrees on 18, and is not applicable on 92. The tool comparison agrees on 43, disagrees on 5, and is not applicable on 141. Non-applicability is distinct from a passed check. The disagreements and missing coverage require further review; these results do not establish that every current percept has been validated.

A separate check compares stored gold options with the bins implied by the recorded reference values. It finds 93 agreements and 0 disagreements, with 108 items outside this numeric check. This verifies consistency between reference values and answer bins; it does not by itself establish that the reference was measured independently of the audio.

A worked case shows what the checks are for. One family asks which of two vessels is taller and which holds more, from the pitch each makes while filling. In an earlier build both halves of the answer were derived from that pitch, which made the gold answer a measurement of the audio rather than an independent one, and on one pair it was simply wrong: two vessels whose ruler heights differ by one centimetre, against a pitch estimate carrying several percent of error, came out in the wrong order. The repair was to take the answer from the ruler alone, to compute volume as a truncated cone rather than a cylinder because only ten of the corpus’s fifty-one vessels are straight-sided to within five percent, and to drop the pairs whose heights are closer together than the pitch can resolve. Nothing about the audio changed; what changed is that the answer no longer comes from the same signal the model is asked to listen to.

These checks address different questions. Rule application checks whether the supplied information leads to the reference answer. Re-measurement and tool comparisons assess whether that information describes the recording. Agreement among them is useful evidence, but it does not replace a documented provenance audit or a human listening study.

IV-C5 Rule authoring

The knowledge string is written once per family and reused across its items. It is checked for item-specific observations and answers. It states the governing relation and the constants it needs, and stops there. Where a quantity is required that is neither hearable nor general, such as a container’s radius, it is supplied in the question, as a given, in every condition alike. This keeps the tell/hear split clean: the question may carry item-specific constants, the knowledge may not, and neither may carry the percept.

IV-C6 Option construction

Items are multiple choice so that a wrong answer is unambiguous and chance is known. All 201 current items have four choices, giving a uniform-guessing chance rate of 25.0%. Options are built in one of three forms according to the question: contiguous bins over the continuous target for absolute estimates, the natural class labels for classification, and ratio bands for comparisons. Bin edges are cut per family, from that family’s own ground-truth values, by a rule with three parts. The three interior edges are placed at midpoints between adjacent ground-truth values; among the placements that keep the four bins near-equal in count, the one chosen is the one that maximizes the smallest distance from any ground-truth value to any edge. The two outer bins are closed and given the width of their neighbour, widened if needed to cover the data. This increases the margin around the reference values and reduces sensitivity to small numerical errors.

One hard constraint governs the cut: the value obtained by applying the family’s rule to the percept sentence alone must land in the same bin as the ground truth. If it does not, either the bins or the item are wrong, and condition ③ would be unanswerable even for a model that did everything asked of it. That constraint is checked for every numeric item (Section IV-C4). The gold option’s position is then balanced across the build so that answer position carries no signal.

IV-C7 Materialization and leak validation

Each admitted item is finally rendered into the four prompts of Table II from the same fields. Condition ④ probes whether the rule and question admit a text-only shortcut. The current implementation reports aggregate no-audio accuracy and does not perform a statistically validated per-item rejection test. Such a gate would require an explicit evaluation protocol, decision threshold and screening record; a single correct multiple-choice response is not sufficient evidence for discarding an item. Consequently, the current build should not be described as certified free of text-only leakage.

IV-D Pairings we rejected

11 pairings were considered and not admitted (Table VI). The pattern is worth stating because it is the main practical finding of the construction effort: audio that is easy to hear and governed by a clean rule is common, and audio whose answer can be checked against something other than itself is rare.

C4 is the single most common cause of rejection, and it fails in two distinct ways. Some candidates fail for circularity: the water level in a filling vessel follows from the resonance the model is being asked to interpret, so a ground truth derived that way would certify only that our estimator and the model agree. Others fail for absence: the delay between a gunshot’s shockwave and its muzzle blast is a clean percept with a clean rule, and no gunshot corpus we found records the shooter’s range. The two are worth separating because only the second can be fixed by finding a better corpus.

The remaining rejections are cheaper to explain. A single-room corpus gives the target quantity one value across every item, so the question has a constant answer. Firearm-model identification is recognition rather than reasoning. Echo delays of two to four milliseconds are below what a listener can resolve, so the percept is not there to be heard whatever the ground truth says.

IV-E Sources under construction

The scarcity described above is the reason the benchmark is being extended by recording rather than by searching. Table VII lists 9 families in progress. Each is set up so that the target quantity is measured by an instrument that never touches the audio, or is fixed when the stimulus is generated: a ruler for a pendulum’s length, hanging calibrated weights for a string’s tension, a laser tachometer for a rotating wheel. Recording our own audio is slower than reusing a corpus and it is the only way we have found to satisfy C4 at scale.

V Experimental setup

V-A Model

We report a preliminary evaluation of Gemini-3.8-flash, accessed through an audio-capable API, over all 201 items and four conditions. This is the only model with complete coverage in the reported results. Evaluations of additional models are in progress and are not included in the comparisons. The protocol requires joint audio and text input and a textual answer, without access to model weights or intermediate representations.

V-B Prompting

Every condition uses one user turn and no system message. The turn is assembled from at most four parts in a fixed order: the rule, the percept sentence, the question, and the options, each separated by a blank line. Condition ① supplies the question and options only. Condition ② prepends the rule. Condition ③ prepends the rule and then the percept sentence, introduced by the words Given (measured from the sound):, so the model can tell the supplied observation from the rule. Condition ④ is byte-identical to ② with the audio file removed from the request. Options are lettered A to D and presented in a fixed order that does not depend on the condition, so the four passes over an item differ only in what is prepended and whether audio is attached.

Each turn asks the model to work through the problem and end with a final line reading Answer: X. The same instruction is used in all four conditions. No few-shot examples are provided, and the template is not tuned separately for each family.

V-C Decoding and scoring

We use temperature 00 and one response per item and condition. These are single-run estimates; the stability of the response labels across repeated API calls has not been measured. The evaluation records truncated and unparseable responses separately. The complete run reported here contains neither, so every condition is scored over all 201 items.

A completed response is scored using the letter on its final Answer: line. If that line is absent, the parser uses the last standalone option letter; if no letter is found, the response is scored incorrect. No partial credit is given, and the reasoning text is not scored. We report accuracy with 95% Wilson intervals. These intervals summarize item-level outcomes within this build; they do not account for dependence among items from the same family.

V-D Baseline validation

Aggregate no-audio accuracy is consistent with chance. With the audio removed but the rule and question intact, Gemini-3.8-flash scores 23.9%, with a 95% Wilson interval containing the 25.0% chance rate (Table VIII). This check does not establish the absence of shortcuts in individual items, nor does it rule out text-only performance by other models. The current results are aggregate baseline evidence, not a per-item leakage certificate.

Percept text produces the larger aggregate gain. Supplying the rule (②) changes accuracy only modestly, while supplying the percept (③) raises it to 98.5%. Since ③ differs from ② only in that the heard quantity is written out, this contrast measures the benefit of the supplied percept representation. Interpreting it as a pure perception deficit additionally requires that the text be complete and preserve the intended application step. Aggregate changes also conceal non-monotonic item-level responses, reported below.

V-E Knowledge-recall probe

A small aggregate gain from supplying the rule could reflect prior knowledge, limited use of the supplied text, or offsetting improvements and regressions. To investigate prior knowledge, we ask one question per family requesting the governing relation and its symbols, without audio, answer choices, or the reference rule. A separate call to the same model, Gemini-3.8-flash, grades the response against the family rule as equivalent, partial, or different. The grading prompt omits the respondent’s identity, but using the same model for answering and grading remains a limitation; these labels have not been independently validated by human annotators.

Table IX groups item accuracy by the family-level probe outcome. The 10 families graded equivalent have a net change of +0.0 percentage points after rule provision; the 5 families graded partial improve by +12.1 points. This association is consistent with greater benefit when the recalled rule is incomplete. It does not prove that the supplied rule was used in a particular response, and zero net change can conceal opposing item-level transitions.

The 3 families graded different show a net change of -8.3 points. A response in this group may state an alternative relation or an incorrect one; the grading scheme does not establish that it is a valid solution route. The probe is therefore supplementary evidence about rule recall, not an independent identification of each item’s failure cause.

VI Analysis

VI-A Failure profiles

Table X assigns every item to the first condition at which the model answers it correctly, and assigns items incorrect under all three diagnostic conditions to application. These are operational labels as defined in Section III-D.

Of the 201 items, 59 are correct without supplied information, 20 first become correct with the rule, and 122 first become correct with percept text also supplied. No item is incorrect in all three diagnostic conditions. This last result does not mean that application never fails: condition ③ still has 3 incorrect answers, each assigned to an earlier group because it was correct under an earlier condition.

Responses are not monotonic. There are 16 items that are correct under ① but incorrect under ②; 18 show a correct-to-incorrect reversal at either adjacent transition. These patterns limit interpretations of the labels as stable internal failure mechanisms. In particular, supplying percept text is not equivalent to improving an audio encoder, so the size of the perception group does not estimate the gain from an encoder replacement.

Sensitivity analyses excluding the flagged contamination case and transformed recordings remain to be completed.

VI-B What the failures depend on

Table XI groups the first-success labels by perceptual axis. Resonant pitch and cycle timing have the largest shares first solved with percept text, while vowel identity has the largest share solved without supplied information.

Some categorical questions may permit direct recognition. For example, a model can name a vowel without explicitly reporting formants, or identify a musical key without enumerating pitch classes. Written responses consistent with these routes motivate a closer audit of criterion C3, but do not establish which computation the model performed. High unaided accuracy alone is not evidence that the stated rule was unnecessary.

By question form, 70% of 46 comparative items are first solved with percept text, compared with 64% of 95 absolute items. Categorical items have the largest unaided success share, 45% of 60. These differences are descriptive: question form, source, and perceptual axis are not independently varied. Further controlled comparisons are needed to attribute them to perceptual difficulty or recognition shortcuts.

VI-C Validation still required

The current evaluation does not include a human listening study. Such a study is needed to test whether the cues are audible, whether percept text is accurate, and whether the supplied rule and observations make the questions answerable. Repeated runs, option permutations and percept paraphrases are also needed to assess the stability of the operational labels. The knowledge-recall probe also requires independent grading and repeated measurements before its labels can support stronger conclusions. Finally, additional sources per perceptual axis and a separate contamination set are needed for cross-source and leak-detection claims.

VII Limitations

  • •

    The percept must be verbalizable. The protocol can only diagnose reasoning whose required observation can be written in a sentence. Percepts that resist short textual description, such as timbre, texture or simultaneous streams, are out of scope by construction, and this excludes much of what audio perception involves.

  • •

    Attribution is behavioural. “Failed perception” means an item becomes solvable once the percept is supplied as text, not that an identified component of the model failed to encode it.

  • •

    Scale and balance. The build is still in progress: several families are small, so per-family intervals are wide, and the family sizes are not yet balanced against each other. 48 of 201 items are a controlled transformation of a real recording rather than an unmodified one. None is synthesized from tones or noise alone; that material was removed from the build.

  • •

    Transformed recordings. Controlled transformations provide known parameters, but may make the stated physical relation easier to apply than in an uncontrolled recording. Performance on these items does not establish the validity of the relation across real acoustic environments.

  • •

    Selection effects. Items were selected using the construction checks, including agreement between extracted percepts and reference values. Results therefore describe this selected set, rather than a random sample of acoustic reasoning tasks.

  • •

    Rule-domain and percept skew. Physics accounts for more than half the items, with music and counting next and phonetics, clinical and signal reasoning represented by a single family each (Table V). Frequency is over-represented among the percepts for the same reason: a quantity that shows up as a pitch, a shift in pitch or a rate is the kind most often paired with an instrument that can measure it independently. Percepts that turn on level, timing or bandwidth are a minority, and the benchmark should not be read as covering audio perception evenly.

  • •

    Percept validation. Percept text is produced by our measurement routines. The stored checks cover 189 of 201 items, with disagreements remaining to be resolved. A systematic human listening study has not been completed.

  • •

    Evaluation scope. Only one model has complete reported results. The probe uses that same model as grader, and label stability has not been tested across repeated runs, option permutations, or percept paraphrases.

  • •

    Release status. Data and code packaging is proposed. Source permissions and final release licences require confirmation, including for transformed audio.

VIII Conclusion

AuDiR evaluates audio reasoning through explicit rule and percept interventions. The current 201-item build supports inspection of both the supplied information and each model’s response pattern. In the preliminary evaluation of Gemini-3.8-flash, supplying percept text produces a much larger accuracy gain than supplying the rule alone. No-audio accuracy is consistent with chance in aggregate. These findings motivate further study of how acoustic observations are used during reasoning, while incomplete percept validation, possible recognition shortcuts and non-monotonic responses constrain stronger attribution. Human validation, additional models and robustness checks are needed before the profiles can reliably guide model improvements.
